utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Bonomy being absent, we sit pursuant to the provisions of Rule 15 bis. Mr. Nice to continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Nice: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We were dealing with the 1990 constitution of Serbia. We had reached in the page numbers at the foot, page 38, and it's article 86. If that could be laid on the overhead projector. To assist the Chamber in the pattern of work for this morning, I have three other constitutions to look at but in each case probably only two or three provisions of each and I will fit other matters that I need to ask this witness around the expirations of the constitutions to a large extent. If we have it on the overhead projector, Article 86 says this: "The President of the Republic shall be elected in direct election and by secret ballot. "The term of the office of the President of the Republic shall be five years. "The same person may be elected for President of the Republic two times only."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Markovic, I think the last thing we discussed last week was who had instructed you to draft this constitution and I think your answer was that no one instructed you to draft the constitution. Have you been able to reflect on that over the weekend and remember who it was who asked you to draft the constitution?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot remember something that does not exist. One can only remember something that was a fact. And let me repeat again: I didn't write the constitution. The constitution was a collective work on the part of the Coordination Commission and then the Assembly which passed it. So I cannot remember something that never existed in the first place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can't help us at all, can you, with who it was that asked the drafting body to draft the constitution at all? And I'm going to suggest that this is a silly answer, but just -- if you're really saying you can't identify who asked you to draft the constitution or who asked the body to draft it. You really can't remember at all?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody asked me to draft the constitution, nor did I write the constitution. The need was shown for a new constitution. Conditions were ripe, and then the body, the Constitutional Commission, as an auxiliary of the Assembly, drafted the constitution. Perhaps that proposal seems to you to be a stupid one, but it corresponds to the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What we see here is the first direct election of the president. Until 1990, the president been appointed by one of the government Assemblies; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until 1990, no, there was no president of the republic at all. The institution didn't exist as such. There was a collective body which was known as the Presidency of the republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so that we can just deal with this thing as a piece, these direct elections, was that simply to bring Serbia in line with similar reforms in the other republics?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The direct elections for the president of the republic provided by this constitution is a component part of the concept of power which permeates this constitution and which in its first articles is formulated. It is the concept of the division of power; the division of power with the parliamentary system of power and with the so-called bicephal executive, that is, two-headed executive organ, bicephalous. One permanent one, which is the head of state, and the other the government which is changeable. And that is the system of government that the Western countries have become accustomed to. And as an example for this constitution we used the Fifth French Republic, dated 1958, which also provides direct election for the head of state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what happened was that, having been elected for five years, the accused went to the polls two years later because of the competitive approach taken by Milan Panic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't tie that up with one man like Milan Panic. Quite simply, a consensus was reached and the president of the federal republic of the day, Mr. Dobrica Cosic, was also of that opinion. He also thought that all the elections should be held at all levels, including elections for the president of the republic. So parliamentary elections and presidential elections, and I think local ones, too, and that was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to debate the detail of that further. That, therefore, took this accused to 1997 by dint of his second term running for five years, and in 1997, one of the various things you did that was controversial, was you sought to interpret this provision, Article 86, as allowing the accused to stand for yet a further term despite the fact that it says in terms the person may only be elected two times only. You said, ah-ha, but since he's only done two years of his first term, the first term doesn't count. That was your argument, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Asked by a journalist first how I understand this provision of the constitution, I just gave an interpretation of it, but since I took part in the writing of the constitution, I'm fully conscious of the fact that there is a void here in the constitution, a gap, and that it says that the mandate of the president of the republic lasts for five years, a five-year term of office. Now, what happens if it lasts for less than five years? Is it considered to be a full mandate? The American constitution, for example, resolved this question by subsequent amendments and said that if a term -- a lesser term was served, then it is not counted as a full term of office. So there's a gap in the constitution here. We needed a provision in this Article 86 which would state that the mandate of the president of the republic, if it be shorter than the full term of office, is counted as having served a full term of office. Had a provision of that kind existed, then there would be no room for interpretation. The situation would have been quite clear. So as I say, we needed a provision here saying that if a lesser period of the five periods [as interpreted] was served, that would be equivalent to a full term of office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The point is, Professor Markovic, that you would do almost anything you could to help this accused. We'll look at the article you speak of so we can deal with this all of a piece. It's Vreme from the 3rd of May, 1997, please. You can have it in the B/C/S, remind yourself of what you said, and we'll see in English on the overhead projector. But you would do almost anything to help this accused stay in office, including advancing the unarguable argument. And on the overhead projector we see what happened, what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, I think you should --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, Mr. Nice just put a proposition to you which you should not leave unanswered. He said that you would do almost anything to help this accused stay in office, including advancing the unarguable argument. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that is not so, any of those statements. I didn't do everything. An individual cannot do everything himself. A candidate has to be put forward as a president of the republic. I cannot elect him or choose him, so I don't agree with Mr. Nice that I cannot back that argument up. Mr. Nice has shown considerable lack of understanding of the constitution of Serbia so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You must not leave unanswered propositions like that when they're put.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if we look at the article, in the second paragraph you're quoted as saying the following: "Same person cannot be elected president of the republic more than twice, but if that person did not complete their full term of office, then this can be seen as if they hadn't been elected at all." And then if we go down the page to the last part of your quotation: "Markovic stated that if the term in office did not last for five years, facts from paragraphs of Article 86 of the Constitution --" I'm so sorry I'm going too fast -- "of Serbia can also be interpreted as if there had been no election at all ..." And then the last sentence you say this: "Election and political justice speak in favour of my interpretation. The factual question is whether the President of the Republic will rely on this interpretation and again run for Presidency or not." Well, now, that's what you said, and you remember one of my earliest questions to you was were you the supreme constitutional lawyer that the accused described you as being. We see here a counter-argument advanced through Vreme by Dr. Pavo Nikolic. Do you accept that he is a constitutional law expert of respectability?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Every professional in constitutional law has the right to his own opinion. There is never a unanimous opinion by all participants in science and among scholars, and here you have it, two different people thinking two different things. It's no heresy. And I didn't give an interview of any kind to the papers that you mentioned. Never. I never gave an interview like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can read the respectable Dr. Nikolic's contrary view, but what happened was this: You didn't press on with -- or the accused didn't press on with your argument, recognised that it was untenable, and therefore he was going to be out of office as President of Serbia, so he simply switched, by removing Lilic, to having himself elected by the federal republic Assembly to become President of the FRY, didn't he? Showing that it didn't really matter which office he held, but that's what he did. He simply switched to the FRY.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These observations incorporated into a question are quite improper, because Mr. Lilic ceased to be president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia when he had served a full term of office to the very last day. He even stayed on several weeks after the expiration of his mandate, which was when I was elected president of Yugoslavia. So to say that Lilic was done away with is a flagrant lie here, because nobody was taken away after he had served -- not served a full mandate. So Mr. Nice must take care of what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What he can comment on as a matter of fact, if he's able to, is whether you simply switched by removing Lilic so that you could then become the President of the FRY. Can you say whether as a matter of fact that was a strategy employed by the accused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no strategy. It was just a spontaneous development of events. The head of state of the day, of the federal state, his mandate had expired pursuant to the constitution, and we had to elect a new head of state. Now, whether immediately afterwards Mr. Lilic was elected, not for president as Mr. Nice just said but as vice-president of the federal government or vice-premier, I can't really remember, but there was absolutely no strategy. Quite simply, the mandate had expired with the passage of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The accused is quite right that Lilic had served his full term. Of course, these constitutions of which you were the draftsman were so malleable -- or you believed them so malleable that anything could have happened if it had been desired, and it was desired that the accused should stay as head of Serbia but he couldn't. So he took the three-year term in the FRY, and then in 2000 there was a further proposal, wasn't there, to change the constitution so that he could stay in for another two full years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you have several questions there, and the first proposition, I think, the witness should attend to because it does say something about him which is adverse as a professional. You say that he was the draftsman and the constitutions were so malleable that anything could have happened if it was desired, and it was desired that the accused would stay as head of state. Did you draft the constitution in such a malleable, such a flexible manner that anything could happen that you desired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course not. And that that is so, if you look at the time after the year 2000, this will be best illustrated that. That constitution, which according to Mr. Nice has qualities of this kind, stayed on for five years once the opposition came into power. And pursuant to that constitution last year, the president of the republic was elected from the ranks of the opposition. So had the constitution been the way Mr. Nice had characterised it, it would have been replaced straight away in the year 2000 once the opposition came to power. So it is the facts and time that show Mr. Nice is not right in his assumptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That disprove him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can probably just see this in tab 14, just the end of this point. While I'm showing this document to you, the position is, therefore, that the -- or as a matter of history, that the accused was President of the FRY until 2000. There were then elections which in fact in any event he lost, but there was -- but there was before an amendment to the constitution. The president's mandate should be by direct election and by secret vote. How many terms and for what period, please?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that, in June, amendments were passed to the federal constitution which did not provide for only that, that is to say that the president of the republic should be elected at direct elections, but it also provided for the direct election of the federal Chamber, that is to say the council of the republic. So this change was far more complex than you are representing it as being. There were a number of amendments, and the president was elected according to that provision for a four-year mandate, and he could be chosen twice to the same position, two terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One way or another, it was going to be possible by the constitutions and the amendments and your proposal in 1997 and the decision made by the accused for him to have stayed in office, had he been elected, until 2008; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, it is not correct, Mr. Nice. You know that for somebody to be in office he has to be elected first. For example, Mr. Milosevic was a candidate and did not win those elections. Therefore --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you're going to do it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go back, then, to the constitution of 1990. And to save time, perhaps we can just look at Article 110 on page 48. This one says in respect of the autonomous province of Kosovo, I think, or Vojvodina, Kosovo now renamed Kosovo and Metohija: "The statute is the highest legal act of the autonomous province which, on the ground of the Constitution, shall lay down the competences of the autonomous province ... "The statute of the autonomous province shall be enacted by its assembly ..." Well, we reminded ourself last week that the Assembly was abolished and never in the event elected again, but even had it been elected, its powers by this constitution, were dramatically reduced even Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in theory from what they would have been under its previous pre-1989 status; correct? Had no constitution, just had an ability to make statutes if the Assembly had even been elected.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Kosovo and Metohija was called Kosovo and Metohija right up until 1968. That was its name. It was only after 1968 that it was referred to as just Kosovo. So its name was Kosovo and Metohija for longer than its name was Kosovo. That's one point. Secondly, in my answers I've already stated that the autonomy, territorial autonomy, was reduced by the 1990 constitution to its classical form, that is to say its classical form and shape, not as a rival to the state in whose composition it was but as a unit realising autonomy within the frameworks and borders of its specific features, within the frameworks of the Republic of Serbia. And Article 13 of the constitutional law for implementing this constitution stated how the Assembly of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija would be constituted. So that is Article 13 that you would have to refer to of the law for the implementation of the constitution. And what you said was correct: The province lost its powers of constitutionality, it enacts a statute, but apart from the former Soviet Union, there was never an autonomous unit in the world which would be able to bring in its own constitution and had the powers of doing that. And our provincial autonomies were introduced in 1945 under the influence of Stalin's constitution of 1936, and their rank is -- was institutionalised in the 1946 constitution. It was mirrored on Stalin's 1936 constitution, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to go into those matters in detail. The constitution that we've been looking at came into effect in September of 1990, and the next things that we can deal with -- incidentally, we've looked at Article 135, and I'm not going to deal with that any more. I may come back to it. Is it right - just yes or no - that about -- that at about this time Slovenia and Croatia were pressing for confederation?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't pinpoint that, the period of time, whether that's when that happened, but I do know that they opted for a confederal system. They were pressing for that, yes, at one point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we return to your exhibit, which was our draft exhibit, the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speaker is kindly asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we return to -- not the draft exhibit, the exhibit marked for identification, Kosovo: Law and Politics, which is marked for identification 818, just so that we can see chronologically what was happening to Kosovo, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the usher would be good enough to place page 89 on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if the witness would like to look at page 88 of this exhibit in Serbian. So we can see what's happening in Kosovo. Here's a decision. A "Decision on the provisional measures for the social protection of self-management rights and social property in the regional radio station in Urosevac." "It is established that at the Regional Radio Station in Urosevac self-management relations have been substantially disrupted, the social interests seriously impaired ..." et cetera. So under II, the director is dismissed and somebody else is appointed in his -- I think Sabani Isa is a man -- I'm in the wrong place. "The provisional executive shall discharge this function full-time and shall take it over immediately ... "III: The Programme Council --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry for the delay, Your Honour. It's my fault entirely. I hadn't given Ms. Dicklich enough advance notice. If the usher would just put the page up a little bit on the screen now so we can see III. "The Programme Council of the Regional Radio Station ... is disbanded." So there's one of the things that's happening following the 1989 changes. A radio station is being taken over by central authority. Is that something that happened a lot in Kosovo, Professor Markovic, taking over news outlets?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I've already explained to you that at the time I did not hold a public office, but temporary measures could have been exercised in the entire territory of the SFRY in accordance with Article 130 of the constitution. So these are not unconstitutional measures. These are temporary measures taken in order to protect public property and self-management system, and that was in compliance with the then self-management system and self-management law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it surprise you if, for example, those resident in Kosovo thought that interference of this kind with the freedom of the press was what was involved?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you as a lawyer should know that I ought to be acquainted with the facts first before I could answer, and I'm not acquainted with the facts. I did not hold a public office at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at another example of the sort of orders that were made. Same document, if we could just go to page 95 for the overhead projector, and it will be 94 for the witness. This is the regime that we're dealing with now, isn't it: "Decision on the enforcement of provisional measures for the social protection of self-management rights and social property in the provincial administration for the advancement of upbringing and education in Pristina." "I: It is established that the self-management relations are gravely disrupted, the public interests seriously impaired and that statutory obligations are not complied with ..." et cetera, et cetera. "II: The executive organ is dismissed: ... director of the Provincial Administration ..." and then somebody else is appointed in his place. Halim Hiseni, it would appear to be probably a Kosovo Albanian name, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you if, first of all, the name of the person sacked, dismissed, would appear to be a Kosovo Albanian name. I imagine you know the difference in general terms between Kosovo Albanian names and others?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what, I couldn't claim with certainty. Because when I was in Rambouillet, I saw that the Gorani, the Roma, and the Ashkali, or rather, the Egyptians have very similar names. So just to give you an example, Qerim Abazi representing the Ashkali was there --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you really are going to tell us that you don't know if this is an Albanian name, I'm going to move on. If that's your answer, you don't know. Just getting things in chronological order. On the 10th of January of 1991, the Constitutional Court of the federal republic affirmed Slovenia's right to self-determination and secession, even if it didn't assert -- didn't accept its right to unilaterally declare secession. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say until I looked at the decision of the Constitutional Court. I need to see the facts, what decision you're talking about. I might have it here with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're pressed for time. Do you have any recollection of this particular decision, Professor Markovic, so as to help us with whether my summary is broadly accurate?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember if we go by dates alone. If you were to give me some more specific details, then perhaps I would be able to recollect if the decision -- if you just tell me that the decision was adopted in January of 1991, then no, I cannot identify the particular decision. You have to tell me what enactment was assessed for its constitutionality, because after all, it was 14 years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In light of the format of your answers and the pressures of time and your wanting to get away, I'm going to move on. We go past Karadjordjevo, with which I've already dealt, and we come to May of 1991. Now, of course you weren't in office, you were just an ordinary member of the SPS, but you were subsequently to be in office of one kind or another for ten years. The Red Berets were established in May of 1991. How was that justified constitutionally? A paramilitary organisation established in May of 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is an improper question because it contains an untruthful claim. There were no Red Berets in May of 1991. Even I wouldn't know about that let alone Professor Markovic. What Red Berets? Who? Where? In May of 1991. It's not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's for the witness to say. Professor, you were asked a question which is in the form of a statement but a question, nonetheless, that the Red Berets were established in May of 1991, and then a subsequent question. What is your answer to the first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is I don't know. I was a university professor. I did not deal with police matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in future, allow the witness to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You were a university professor, but subsequently you were a member of the Assembly of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and then you were a Deputy Prime Minister. Now, one of the powers of the Assembly of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was that it had to approve the federal budget. Just yes or no so that we can understand the picture: Did you, as a member of the Assembly, acquainting yourself with and approving the federal budget, ever approve money for something such as the Red Berets, of which, of course, you're aware?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, the Federal Assembly, just as any other parliament in the world, adopts or approves the budget. The budget is a very detailed enactment, full of figures, and while I was a deputy, I didn't really look into those figures because every ministry and every federal agency was just an item within the budget. So I didn't really look into the figures. I only looked into my fields, the fields for my domain, such as education, culture, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, these are all very serious matters, and the existence of the body called the Red Berets was known. If it was financed even in part by federal body, perhaps Mr. Kertes' federal customs office, this is something of which you Assembly members should have oversight, isn't it, or was it hidden from you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the eve of the adoption of budget, minister of finance would always give a presentation, and I never heard while I was a deputy in the Federal Assembly him mentioning any expenditures for the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we take it if the Judges in due course find that the funding came in part from the federal budget, that it was hidden from the view of those who should have been supervising the propriety of the payment? May we take that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we couldn't take that. We should take a look at the budget, the specific budget for those years, check the items, because it's very difficult now to recollect items. Some items were expressed very -- in very global terms, such as "expenditures" without specifying expenditure for what. We should check, look into each budget item, check the figures for that item and see whether the Red Berets were provided for within that item. I don't have such a memory as to be able to remember all budgetary items.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... this way. You've been, of course, following events in the country of which you were an office-holder and to some degree following events in this trial. When you've heard of the activities of the Red Berets, realising that they had to be funded from either Serbia or the federal republic, were you shocked at what you had been a party to?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where you come with this idea that I was -- that I had been a party to that. What do you mean I was a party, I was a member of the Red Berets, that I wore a red beret on my head; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a legislator approving a budget at a time when paramilitaries were operating on the territory of other states, where tens and hundreds of thousands, or tens of thousands of people and over a hundred thousand people eventually lost their lives, were you shocked at discovering what you and your fellow legislators had been a part of?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat once again that I don't know that there ever was an item for Red Berets within the budget. You should present it here as evidence so that I could see it. As far as I can remember, up until 1996, while I served as a federal deputy, I never saw such an item in the federal budget.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the Professor has been clear on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reason I pressed you on it is this, Professor: We've had evidence in the form of Exhibit 390, tabs 9 and I think 11, which are excerpts from the JSO video film, we've had evidence, Professor Markovic, that Frenki Simatovic says that something called the JSO was constituted on the 4th of May of 1991, and you in your evidence-in-chief, and I think it was under tab 3, drew to our attention the Constitutional Court's condemnation of paramilitary activity by reference to the ZNG. What I'd like your help with as the constitutional expert and as the participating member of the Assembly and subsequently a Deputy Prime Minister is why there was never any constitutional or other legal condemnation of the Red Berets, the JSO known later as the Red Berets. Can you help us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is truly improper. The -- according to the information available here, the JSO were established in 1996. I don't care who stated what. This is an improper way to put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not for the accused to try and assist the witness. The evidence is absolutely clear, as the Chamber will remember, in the words of Simatovic addressed to this accused at the ceremony subject of the videotape. And just to remind the Chamber and the accused, what Simatovic says on the videotape is this: "It -" by which he was referring to the JSO - "was constituted on the 4th of May, 1991, at the time of break-up of the former Yugoslavia and since it emerged has constantly worked to protect the national security in circumstances where the existence of the Serbian people was directly jeopardised throughout its entire ethnic area."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice -- Professor, let me put the question to you in this way: Were you aware of the activities of the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can move on. The coincidence of time, 4th of May, from that exhibit, to the Red Berets, 26th of June for the ZNG, and Defence tab 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, you were to be elected to the Federal Assembly. What month of what year did that take effect?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was elected in late December, I believe it was the 23rd or the 24th of December, 1992. And I remained in that position until September 1996, when the new Assembly was elected, the new Federal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the middle and early autumn or autumn of 1991, there was a political initiative coming from the accused known as the Belgrade initiative. Are you aware of that? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the substance of it. The name is familiar, but I cannot remember the substance of that initiative. After all, it's been 14 years. Perhaps if you were to give me some additional details, then I would be able to remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... incorporate within the residual state as much as possible but in particular to incorporate Bosnia as well as Serbia and Montenegro within the remaining Yugoslavia; correct? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember the substance of that initiative at all. I did not participate in any capacity in drafting that document and cannot remember the actual contents of it, so I'd better not say anything for fear of saying something that is not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us turn to the next constitution I think you were involved in. It's the constitution of Republic of Serbian Krajina, RSK, and we'll lay that on the overhead projector for you. Can you remember when this constitution took effect, Mr. Babic's constitution?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen it, and that's why I quoted the words of Lord Palmerston. I never saw that constitution, nor do I know its contents. I spoke to you about the statute of the Serbian Autonomous Region. I know nothing about the constitution of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain, then, what it was you were doing for Mr. Babic, because Mr. Babic in evidence said quite clearly that it was drafted by Borivoj Rasua and Professor Ratko Markovic.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he referred to. I really don't know what he referred to. First of all, Borivoj Rasua, as far as I know, is not a lawyer at all. Somebody who is not a lawyer cannot draft a constitution. I told you that we assisted with the drafting of the statute of the Serbian Autonomous Region. I assisted and Academician Jovicic. However, that was the statute of an autonomous region. I don't know how the text of the constitution was drafted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And indeed it's true that it was first a statute and then it was proclaimed a constitution. So let's see if this document in the parts I want you to look at jogs your memory. On the first page will be page 2 of 37 for the English, and it's at the top of the page. Thank you very much. And it reads -- I hope you have it in the Serbian. "Proceeding from the right of the Serb people to self-determination and in compliance with the free will of the Serb people in the Serb Autonomous District of Krajina, expressed at a referendum, as well as the centuries old struggle of the Serb people for the freedom of its liberate, democratic and governmental tradition, resolve to establish a democratic state of the Serb people in their historic and ethnic areas in which other citizens will be enabled to exercise their ethnic rights, a state based on sovereignty which belongs to the Serbian people and other citizens in it, on the rule of law and equal rights for the prosperity of all individuals and society, the Serb people of Republika Srpska Krajina, through their representatives in the Constitutional Assembly, proclaim ..." There's no legal -- and first of all, does this jog your memory? Did you draft this bit in the statute which you helped create?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. This provision was a very brief one. It contained perhaps 20 articles, and it was modelled after the statutes of autonomous units. As far as I can see, this is an entire constitution, a full constitution. It contains everything that a constitution should contain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to page 3 of 37.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have that document, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You do have the document, Your Honour. It's Exhibit 351, tab 68, and I apologise for not having mentioned that already. But if we can go to page 3 of 37. Indeed Article 5 is what I'm looking for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The territory of the Republika Srpska Krajina is integral and inviolable. A change to the borders of Republika Srpska Krajina can only be decided by its citizens at a referendum. "The Assembly of the Republika Srpska Krajina can decide that other Serb territories be joined to the Republika Srpska Krajina should the citizens of such territories decide to join the Republika Srpska Krajina." Was that an article, one of ten or thereabouts, that you drafted?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say now because this pertains to the territory of a state, whereas the other document pertained to an autonomous region. However, I don't see anything unusual here. I don't see why you read it in such dramatic tone. Simply stated, the Serb people did not wish to be made to leave Yugoslavia. This is a reaction to the secession of Croatia. So why should there be anything dramatic here? Simply speaking, the Serb people who constituted in that area a majority did not wish to go and live in Croatia in a state where they would be an ethnic minority and where they would not feel at home. What is unnatural about this provision?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not here as an expert, but I can at least ask you this: Do I take it, then, from your answer that you, you personally think that what they were doing was entirely legal, to carve out a portion of a state that was to be recognised by the European Union? Is that what you thought was legal?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just as legal as Croatian secession from the federal Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you just help us, again not as an expert but as a matter of fact, just by pointing us, please, to the differences between the rights of the people, the Serbs in Croatia, from the rights of the Kosovo Albanians in Serbia where they were, of course, an 85 per cent majority? Can you just point us to the factual difference between the two so that we can follow it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I can. The difference is very simple. The Serb people is a constituent people in the Republic of Croatia. The Albanian people is a national minority in the Republic of Serbia. The right to self-determination is something that belongs to a constituent people, not an ethnic minority, because an ethnic minority already has its mother state, and that's the Republic of Albania.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, please -- sorry. We've understood that, as you've explained that before, but it certainly constitutes this, doesn't it: In terms of ethnic groups, totally different rules, in your mind, apply for ethnic Albanians from ethnic Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, he has explained why.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 28 of 37, Article 102, please. "The Armed Forces of the Republika Srpska Krajina are the territorial defence of the Republika Srpska Krajina." Now, by whom were they paid, Professor Markovic? You were on the Assembly of the federal republic from 1992. Help us, please, and indeed those viewing so they can know, by whom were these armed forces paid?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. As a separate item in the budget, they were not expressed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have heard a little, and we are going to hear a great deal more about things called the 30th and 40th personnel centres, established through the Supreme Defence Council. Professor Markovic, you know what the Supreme Defence Council was?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I do, but I wasn't a member in order to know what decisions it made, but I know what kind of organ it was. It was a body that commanded the army of Yugoslavia, and ex officio two republican presidents and the federal president were members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know about the 30th and 40th personnel centres?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm hearing about them for the first time from you now. I had never heard about it before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How, then, did you think that these Serbs outside Serbia and the federal republic were able to sustain an armed force, because you must have learnt that they had armed forces?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, if I -- if I'm a factual witness, I do not know that. I do not know the facts. I can only give you my assumptions, my suppositions, but that's not my job here. I do not know the facts. At the time, I repeat, I was a university professor, and from 1992 on, I was a federal MP, one among a hundred or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll come back to that. Before -- The Hague Conference, are you acquainted, as a member of the public or as somebody later in government viewing the history of your state, are you acquainted with what happened at The Hague Conference?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed I do.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time, a certain plan was made. Lord Carrington made a plan to resolve the crisis in Yugoslavia, and as far as I remember, that plan was not accepted by everybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because you drew to our attention at tab 2 of your exhibits the letter to -- or an answer to Lord Carrington's question, and I wondered what your particular role in relation to that letter was. Can you help us? Maybe it was a bit of expert evidence to comment on legality or illegality. Just help us. What was your -- what was the significance for you of the letter to Lord Carrington?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Lord Carrington addressed a letter to the Arbitration Committee, which was an auxiliary working body of the conference, and the Arbitration Commission addressed the organs in all Yugoslav republics, asking for their opinions. One of those organs was the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia, therefore a federal body. The Arbitration Commission elicited the opinion of federal bodies as well. And in response to this request by the Arbitration Commission, the Constitutional Court wrote that letter at one of its sessions and sent it to the Arbitration Commission. So it is a letter, a document from the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we are looking at things chronologically and at the significance, if any, of that answer, and if there's any reliance by you on behalf of this accused as to the illegality of other acts by other states, shouldn't we bear in mind that the first act of force was the log revolution, to which we referred last week, and that either the first or one of the first acts of violence was the arming of the Serbs, if it happened, in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the log revolution cannot be put before the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia in order to assess its constitutionality. The only thing that can be assessed by the Constitutional Court for constitutionality are federal enactments and the federal constitution. Log revolutions are material, substantive acts, and they cannot be assessed for legality or constitutionality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I may come back to some documents, if I have time, for the end of 1991, but can you just confirm from memory that there was an offer by the European Union to all states of the former Yugoslavia to see if they -- what they were seeking by way of independence? Do you remember that being made on the 16th or 17th of December of 1991? We're going to see another reference to it and it's also contained in the Cassese article that you were going to produce but weren't able to, but do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, correct. I remember. It was exactly the way you said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the clear consequence of that was that Bosnia was going to go for independence. And so that we can have everything in a chronological way, once it was known that Bosnia was going for independence, the Belgrade initiative, which involved the incorporation of Bosnia, was dead. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat to you, the Belgrade initiative fell into complete oblivion, in my mind. I cannot remember the substance of the Belgrade initiative, although the name rings a bell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to make our position as the Prosecution clear, it was following the acceptance by Bosnia of the European Union's invitation that it became necessary for the accused to try one other way, having an enlarged Serbia, and that was with his third Yugoslavia, the so-called third Yugoslavia for which there was a conference at the beginning of 1992. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which conference you are referring to. It would be very good if I could read that paragraph of the indictment, because things would be much clearer to me then, and I could memorise it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have my eye on the clock, and I'll come back possibly to that a little later. Can we go back to marked for exhibit -- marked for identification Exhibit 818 briefly and just see again some of the things that happened either at the end of 1991 or in 1992 to Kosovo, and we'll look at another constitution so we can get the picture. We go to page 69 of this exhibit in the English, which I expect will be 68 for you, and indeed it is. We can see that the elementary education law requiring the language of instruction to be Serbian and nationalities to be provided with education in the mother tongue if not less than 15 pupils enroll in the first grade, subject to the consent of the Ministry of Education. It's on page 69. Then we -- that was the elementary education law at the top of the page, Usher. And then we're coming down to the middle of the page, the secondary education law: "The school shall conduct instruction in the Serbian language. "The school shall follow the syllabus of the language of nationalities or bilingually when not less than 15 pupils of the same grade opt for it ..." Then at the bottom of the page, the high school law: "Higher education shall be acquired in the Serbian language. "Instruction at a high school may be in the languages of nationalities or national minorities and in one of the world languages decided by the founder." Is this, do you think, oppressive to Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. Simple arithmetics go in the face of your argument. They fulfil the requirement of 15 in all the three levels of school. We are talking about much smaller minorities than Kosovo Albanians here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go over to page 107, for you page 106. All about the same time, in the same year. The law on Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts: "The Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts is the supreme scientific and artistic institution in the Republic of Serbia. "The Academy of Sciences and Arts of Kosovo and Metohija shall terminate its work as of the day of entry into force of the present law ..." If you'd like to turn over -- that's as far as I need go for these purposes, I think. What do you think that would have done to a place 85 per cent of the same ethnic origin, having to close the doors on its academy? And indeed the next reference is to the Institute of Kosovo History, which had to terminate its work. Is this all to do with constitutionality, or is this to do with centralising Serbian state and oppressing Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I think that a small country like Serbia does not have enough people to fill three academies of science. At the time there were three academies of science. The requirements for becoming a member of the academy are extremely high, and in the Republic of Serbia, there are simply not enough personalities of respectability that could fill three academies. Much bigger states, like France, have only one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and its institute of history had existed and had functioned, and now for no good reason, it may be thought, they were simply being abolished. I mean, I know you were only a member of the party at the time, but can you help us with why that really was done? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here is why: We simply moved to a different concept of autonomy. Autonomy is not a quasi-state. It is a unit with a territorial autonomy. And that goes with certain other changes regarding other institutions, like academies of science. If it is a territorial unit with a degree of autonomy, scientists from that unit can be elected members of the Academy of Science of Serbia. And indeed, the Academy of Science of Serbia had members both from Kosovo and Metohija and from Vojvodina, the other autonomous unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A very brief look at the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, please, which Your Honours have had produced twice as either Exhibit 319, tab 1, or as Exhibit 132. And do you remember, Professor Markovic, the passage of your evidence that appeared to have been incorrectly interpreted where you claimed privilege from identifying your involvement in the drafting of a constitution? We've looked at the RSK for which you say you contributed something in respect of a law, and we're now looking at the constitution of the RS. Which one of these was it that you were referring to when you were, right at the beginning of your evidence, saying you were privileged from discussing it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say I was privileged from discussing it. I said it would not be fair for me to speak about it, and I meant the constitution of the autonomous region. And by the way, in my testimony I enumerated all the constitutions to which I contributed. This one would be the fifth. According to you, you would make me out to be the main constitution writer for the Balkans. It looks as if I had written them all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you involve yourself in the preparation, assistance, drafting of this constitution or any statute that preceded it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in any way, and I explained why. Bosnia and Herzegovina or, rather, Republika Srpska has enough qualified professors, some of them members of the Academy of Science, that they are able to do it without any assistance from outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I may come back to ask you some questions about that if time permits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But can we look, please, Usher, simply at page 1 of this constitution, Article 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will see the family of constitutions involving the Serbs of the former Yugoslavia. Article 2 says: "The territory of the Republic consists of regions of Serbian ethnic entities including the regions where genocide has been committed upon the Serbian people. "The borders of the Republic shall be established and altered by means of plebiscite of a three-quarter majority of the total number of registered voters. "The Republic is part of the federal state of Yugoslavia." What does that mean? Of which federal state was the RS proclaiming itself, the RS there from -- cut out from Bosnia, of what Yugoslavia was it proclaiming itself to be part?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That same Yugoslavia to which it had belonged until then. Quite simply, the Serbian people in areas where it was in the majority did not wish to be led out into foreign states, states that they did not feel as their own, states in which they would be an ethnic minority. It was a struggle for preserving the old Yugoslavia, not for creating some sort of Greater Serbia. Those people simply didn't want to be led out. They wanted to stay in their former state. It is a natural aspiration. They wanted to stay together with their own people in the same mother-state in which they had lived until then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Article 4 says: "The Republic may enter into union with state forms of other peoples constitutive of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Did that mean other Serb-dominated areas?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why you address me personally, as if I had written this. You should ask something like, "Do the authors mean ..." or something like that. I can only interpret this as a lawyer, just like you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Finally, over the page to Article 9. "The capital city of the Republic of Sarajevo." You were an Assembly member starting at the end of 1992. We all know about the siege of Sarajevo. Does the desire to have Sarajevo as the capital, in your judgement as a former parliamentarian and later Deputy Prime Minister, explain the siege?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the -- both capacities that you ascribe to me I did not have on the 16th of March, 1992. I was neither the federal MP or Deputy Prime Minister. At that time, I was only a university professor. Do you want my opinion as a university professor, because I'm a factual witness here? But then it would not --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want your knowledge --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- be proper testimony it would just be my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... an Assembly member from 1992, please. That's what I want.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became a federal MP in end 1992. I believe our term of office was verified only in February 1993. And you know that one can only become an MP once their office, their election is verified by the parliament. I can only give you an opinion as a man in the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally on this constitution, at page 17. For example, 110, Article 110: "Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina shall have its own Army, consisting of standing units and reserve units." Throughout its life and for the period of time when you were an Assembly member, are you aware how the RS was -- the army of Republika Srpska was funded?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again I'll return to that with time. I want you now, please, to look at the next constitution that you drafted, the last of -- sorry. I realise you're saying you had no part in the previous one. The next constitution with which you had any part in the drafting was the 1992 FRY constitution. That came to be prepared in 1992, I think in April. Now, if you'd look, please, at this document, you'll find it's an article -- again it's entirely my fault. I -- I hadn't given Ms. Dicklich advance notice of what I'm going to be putting to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, while it's coming, and I don't know how Your Honours are committed over the break, but it's a document that it may be of value for you to spend -- maybe worthwhile spending time with it over the break, assuming we can find it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it right that there was, in January of 1992, European recognition of Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it right, following that, that there was a meeting on the 5th of February of 1992 in Podgorica for the purpose of considering the 1992 constitution that was to come?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to take my word for it if I say that I don't know about that, because I was not present at the meeting. I was not part of the delegation from the Republic of Serbia. I know that for sure, and I know even the reasons why I wasn't on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was it that you came to be involved in drafting the 1992 constitution?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again as an expert. I was a member of that narrower body that had prepared a draft constitution, and that body was made up following the principle of equal representation. Half of the members were from Serbia, half from Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who instructed you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, nobody gave me any instructions. And if someone were there to give me instructions, then they would be best placed to write the constitution themselves. I assume that the people drafting this had their own autonomy and can do so themselves, where it is the facts that define the contents and substance of a constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we're coming to the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I seem to have mislaid this particular document I wanted you to read, and I'm afraid I can't ask you to read it over the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The exhibits produced earlier, may they be given numbers? There was the Vreme article, and there was an amendment. If the Vreme article could be numbered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it may be numbered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Before it's admitted into evidence I do have several objections, which I can outline briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Firstly, in evidence the witness stated himself that he had never given an interview like that. He didn't accept that he'd given the interview. Secondly, in my submission, it adds nothing to the evidence he's actually already given to the Court, and on analysis of the article, it appears that it is not even an original interview but was in fact material taken from Politika Ekspres and, before that, Tanjug. My concern, Your Honour, is firstly, as I've stated, it adds nothing; and secondly, it contains journalistic comment, and other names are referred to in the B/C/S version of the article which has not been translated its entirety. As far as I can establish, just five paragraphs of the original article has been translated for these purposes. The fear is also that there is included comment by someone else - Professor Nikolic - who was not a witness in this case. Your Honour, briefly those are my observations on the admissibility of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could we sever the comments?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the difficulties there are paragraph -- the last paragraph relating to Professor Nikolic could be severed, but the concerns remain in terms of the originality of the interview and the concerns about this witness admitting and stating that he never gave an interview like that. So my concerns still stay, but if Your Honour is willing to and wants to admit it, then I would ask that the comments from Professor Nikolic go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness acknowledged the views expressed there as being no different from his own, and the value is very substantially in the comments of Nikolic, given the way this witness has been advanced as an unimpeachable and peerless expert, we see here, as he was obliged to concede, public expression of contrary views on important matters, and if I have time, we're going so see more. And therefore, given the assertion that I've made that this witness would do whatever was necessary to help this accused, it's important to see that his opinions were indeed the subject of contrary academic expert opinion. So in our submission, the article is admissible for both parts and on the normal grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On the basis that the professor acknowledged that these -- the views expressed are similar to his, we'll admit the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 823.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful. The other document doesn't need to be produced in the event the witness gave answers that are sufficient and I needn't burden the record with a document. As to the document I was going to ask you to look at over the adjournment, it's entirely my error. Ms. Dicklich had, of course, produced it but I gave her a wrong internal reference. Can I now distribute to the Chamber, to the witness, and to the accused and to Ms. Higgins an article written by this witness. The first thing we'll see -- I'm going to require a lot of it to be shown, so if the usher could stay by the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that the interpreter misspoke, because it says in Serbian that this is a text written by the accused whereas I can see on the transcript it says that the text was written by the witness. So that was a slip of the tongue. But just to put that right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look, Professor Markovic, at the top of the page, and the Chamber can see this in the translation, it is headed Pravni Zivot 3-4/92. Would that suggest that this article was written in or about March or April 1992, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what it ought to mean, and that they are published on time, but usually they're published a little late, and then the copies are antedated, the issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 1992 FRY constitution is dated the 27th of April. So that would mean that you were writing or preparing this article either at the time of drafting of the constitution or shortly before; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they worked on that text from February, and it was adopted in parliament on the 27th of April, 1992, but it was worked on before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, it only took five days to draft the FRY constitution, so it is said. Is that a correct proposition? We'll see the proposition later.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you take a look at expired labour, you cannot write the constitution and be an ignoramus. If you look at past labour, past labour, you would have to have 15 years of knowledge accumulation in order to be able to write it in the space of just five days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it, in fact, written in five days? Please help us.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The draft constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was written. That is to say, those republics who had decided to remain within the then-state of Yugoslavia and to carry on its continuity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, this text which may actually merit detailed reading, is unrevised. It's an official translation but it is unrevised. There are some passages of it which are quite awkward, but for the most part I think it's easily to be followed and much of it I'd like to deal with but I have limited time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 1, from about three lines down, reads as follows: Since the 1968 constitutional amendments -" and I'm going to miss out words from time to time to save time - "Serbia has been engaged in a struggle to have as many states on the territory of its republic, as other republics, members of the Yugoslav Federation have on theirs. That struggle successfully ended only in 1990 by drafting the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia." Next sentence on the same paragraph: "... unification of Serbia and formation of a unique state government on its entire territory is the greatest result of this Constitution." Is that something to which you still -- is that something you still believe, Professor Markovic? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... of centralisation of Serbia, achieved by the 1990 constitution, isn't it, unification of Serbia and a formation of a unique state government. That's what this was all about.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with you there. Decentralisation existed on two counts; territorial autonomy and local self-government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the professor to explain this, that since 1968 -- "Since the 1968 constitutional amendments to the SFRY Constitution from 1963, Serbia has been engaged in a struggle to have as many states on the territory of its republic, as other republics, members of the Yugoslav Federation have on theirs." The part I would like to have comment on is "to have as many states on the territory of its republic ..." What does that mean? And Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. then, "as other members --" "as other republics have." First, what is meant by "as many states on the territory of its republic," and how is that contrasted with the situation of other republics?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this meant that the Republic of Serbia should undertake all the prerogatives of its state power and authority throughout its territory like the other five republics, whereas the autonomous units should just realise their autonomy within the frameworks of the Republic of Serbia itself. Because the status of the autonomous provinces beginning with 1968, for instance, pushed Serbia back to an area -- as a state, I'm saying -- to an area between the autonomous provinces, lodged there. The autonomous provinces were the protagonists of their own constitution, their own laws, they had their own government, their organs of administration, their own Supreme Court, their own Constitutional Courts. So the Republic of Serbia was not a state on the territory of the autonomous provinces. It wasn't a united state on its own territory and did not have the prerogatives of its own social powers like the other five republics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So in effect it meant to have incorporated within the territory of Serbia the autonomous states, the autonomous provinces.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That meant that the autonomous provinces were supposed to be deprived of the state functions that they gradually won since 1968. For example, in 1968 itself, when this status of the autonomous provinces came into being as quasi-republics, this was being built up, they had the right to a constitutional law which they had never enjoyed until then. Then they enjoyed the right to a statute as the highest act, and the right to enact laws, which it never had until 1968. It also gained a Supreme Court, which it did not have the right to before that. The Assembly and the Executive Council of the autonomous province was vested with the right to take proceedings with the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia, for instance, which right it did not have up until then, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next part of the question is how was Serbia in a position of inequality in that regard in relation to the other republics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first of all, it was in a position of inequality, let me repeat, because the functions of the state could be realised just outside the territory of the provinces themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you able to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And secondly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you able to illustrate the inequality by saying, for example, what the position was with Croatia or Slovenia or any other republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other republics had all the prerogatives of state power and authority throughout their territory. The laws were in force throughout the territory of the republic, for example, as was the constitution. The republican constitution and the republic as a whole was represented in the federal state. And in the federal state Serbia was represented itself, that is to say this space or area between the two provinces and the provinces themselves separately. So they were not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've had a note, which I suspect comes from one of the interpretation booths, where they say having compared the Serbian and the English, that fifth line down, the phrase "as many states" is better translated as "as much of a state."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. "As much of a state." I see. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're much obliged to the booths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That would explain the difficulty I had, yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I say, Professor Markovic, generally about this article, my suggestion is to you overall that this article in a sense gives the game away and reveals in many ways exactly the thinking of the political leadership of Serbia at this critical time of 1992, and that even if, as you say, nobody asked you to write the constitution, you nevertheless happened to understand what the thinking of the leadership was and indeed how it was going to be executed. So, so that you have that in mind, that's my general proposition, shall we look at the first footnote, the double starred footnote, "Publishing the text of the author who directly worked in the project of the Constitution of the joint state of Serbia and Montenegro, among other things, has a primary goal to inspire our wise constitutional thinkers and our experts, to publish in their views on the constitutional status of Serbia and its orientation to create joint state, with perspective of graduate unification of all Serbian states and Serbian people on the pages of this magazine." That is the clearest exposition of a plan to create an enlarged Serbia to which other Serb areas could join. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're not correct, on that on two counts, for two reasons. First of all, I didn't write this. This was written by the editorial board of that scientific journal, magazine. The editorial board and not me as author. And secondly, you're not right because there were no efforts to create a Greater Serbia. The effort was to remain within Yugoslavia and not to leave Yugoslavia. So the Serb people did not wish to borrow their ethnic substance to anyone else and to create a state of their own based on the Serb people alone. Why would the Croatian state be created of the Serb people or Bosnia created of the Serb people? They wanted to stay where they were. They didn't wish to leave. They wished to remain in the state they had lived in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll see what you say later in the article. In the English to page 2, and in your text, Professor, to page 374, first paragraph. "However, since the Federation that was first created by the amendments from 1971 ..." and then amended and so on, "... which at the time of the enactment of the constitution of Serbia ... became openly separatist, Serbia had to integrate security mechanisms in its Constitution in case of already visible forms of disregard of the federal legal system and other violations of the Federal Constitution to the cost of the Republic of Serbia. By proclaiming itself -" and then that's a reference to the Article 135 - "a part of the SFRY, the Republic of Serbia stipulated in its Constitution that she would realise the rights and duties she has according to its Constitution ..." And I'm going to read to the end the paragraph from the next sentence: "Therefore, to avoid the possibility that some vital government functions would not be executed because of separatism and the republics cancelling their participation in the work of federal bodies, the Republic of Serbia -" and this is perhaps a passage that is a little awkward as presently translated - "envisaged these functions in its Constitution as its own, prolonging their exercise until the SFRY and the Federal Constitution exist. From a legal point of view, this provision is useless, even incorrect in relation to the Federation and its Constitution. However, it is an expression of a specific political situation and actual relations in the Federation, and Serbia could not influence the outcome." Two things. Aren't you really saying there that Serbia's 1990 constitution was in defiance of the law, claiming that this was because of already present disregard or separatism?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which law you're referring to. You say that the Serbian constitution was in defiance or contrary to the law. Which law?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the federal constitution of 1974, which was the abiding law at the time by which constitutional change was permitted.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not necessary for it to say the constitution of the federal unit, that the rights and units of the federal state will be realised within it, within the federal state. But in view of the express tendencies towards secession, the constitution repeated that. That is to say, it said that all the functions, rights, and duties which it provides for the Republic of Serbia, envisaged for the Republic of Serbia, which the federal constitution had envisaged for the federation would be realised within the federation, that is to say within the federal state. And in view of the dangers of secession, those rights and duties were repeated as the rights and duties of the Republic of Serbia. However, it deferred their implementation until the constitution of 1974 was still in force, or its successor, the 1992 constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
