utterances.text: You see, I'm not going to explore the detail of that answer now, but dealing with the second point, the justification for this, the Serbian constitution was dated September 1990, and by that time what separatism had there actually been apart from, say, the summer log revolution or the arming of Serbs in the Krajina? Where is the separatism which you rely on in this article? Or, as I'm going to suggest, is this a form of post facto justification?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was said here that leading questions are not allowed, so why are you suggesting an answer to me now? We're talking about amendments to the constitution of the Republic of Slovenia, which were enacted in 1989, and we dealt with those amendments here. We examined them. And in one of the provisions of those amendments, it was stated that the right to self-determination, including the right to secession, that the Republic of Slovenia would regulate in its constitution, and that was in 1989. And it was the first decision that the Constitutional Court took, and we discussed here. And the constitution of the Republic of Serbia, the 28th of September, 1990 is the date of that. And as far as I can say, the reactions on the constitution of Serbia was a posteriori, that is to say once we had clear manifestations of aspirations towards the right to self-determination as being the right to secession as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, the prohibition against leading questions only applies to examination-in-chief and re-examination. It doesn't apply to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we go on to page 3 in the English, and to the paragraph in your text, Professor, which is on page 375, on the right-hand side, under II: "Since its resurrection (1804), the modern Serbian state should have solved its most important question - how to gather Serbian people, dispersed during the five centuries of foreign power, in one state, in other words, how should the Serbian state be a protector of all Serbs. During the XIX century, when the medieval Serbian state was rebuilt, many wise Serbian people and Serbian political parties ... tried to solve that problem with their programs for unification ..." That's a reference to Nacertanije, I think. But the first sentence is the clearest possible exposition of what was then, in 1992, the political leadership's plan to gather all Serb people in one state. Am I not right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're not right because the Serb people already existed in a single state, and the name of that single one state was Yugoslavia. And the struggle of the Serbian people, in fact, is the wrong thesis. It wasn't the struggle to create a Greater Serbia but to preserve Yugoslavia. Serbia was the largest country when it was Yugoslavia, when all the Serbs lived in one state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, by 1992, that's all history. Secessions have happened and international recognition has taken place, and the problem is what's going to happen to the Serbs with their proclaimed but unrecognised states in Croatia and in Bosnia? And my suggestion to you, and I give you one last chance to think about it, is that writing this in 1992 is the clearest reflection of the accused's and the other political leadership's intention to create a new state for all Serbs by carving out from and then attaching to Serbia parts of Croatia and Bosnia. Correct or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's an important question, Professor, because that is the thesis of the Prosecution. That's the Prosecution case in essence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, this is a text written by an author and not written by Mr. Milosevic. I myself wrote this text, and it says that the entire text was printed in a scholarly, scientific journal which is called Legal Life. And there is an asterisk with my name stating my functions. So I wrote this in the capacity of a professional scientific worker, not a man of politics because I had no political functions at the time. That's the first point. The second point is this: There was no creation of a new state, as you put it. It was simply the preservation of the old state, the SFRY or, rather, federal Yugoslavia. That is to say the whole question lies in this point: It wasn't an effort on the part of the leadership of Serbia to create a Greater Serbia but to preserve and maintain Yugoslavia, because the Serbs from the secessionist republics did not wish to go and live in another state that they didn't experience and feel to be their own. They wanted to remain living in the country they had always lived in for the past 70 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Allow me to try to bring you back to the question. Secession and international recognition had already happened, so that what you set out here could only be achieved by bringing into the Serb fold, in due course, those parts of the territories of Croatia and Bosnia which could be dominated or ruled by Serbs. Am I not right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, Mr. Nice, I'm talking about the 19th century, not the 20th century.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's look at the next paragraph, still on your page 375, because I'm going to suggest to you that in the next -- in this paragraph and the following one you completely reveal the realities of what we're inquiring into. You said this: "That question is a permanent national task, still unsolved. Only in this century, for the third time Serbian people was put in a position when they have to solve their fundamental national question - how to organise their state. As in previous two situations of this century, even now Serbian people have two options. The first one proceeds from the mixing of nations on the South-Slav territory. There are compact territories where one nation is in majority, but there are also some enclaves, which are smaller territories, populated by one nation and surrounded from all sides by one or many other nations. Furthermore, there are territories where no nation has a total majority. Proceeding from such a reality, which is primarily the reality of Serbian people, a joint state of all Yugoslav nations organised as a complex state, specifically, as a federal state, is considered to be mostly in accordance with." Just pausing there. From the questions I asked you before the break and in particular from the questions about the change from the Belgrade initiative to the third Yugoslavia turning around the invitation of the European Union, the Yugoslav states to declare independence, this was an impossible -- there was no longer possible, because Croatia had gone, Slovenia had gone, and Bosnia had gone. So that what you've set out in the paragraph until this full stop is impossible. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a statement to the effect that the federation of Yugoslav peoples is the optimum way to resolve the Serbian national question as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We understand that's the Serbian view, but here you are winter 1991/1992, or spring 1992, with reality facing you, describing the options, and you go on to say this: "A federation -- a confederation would not be a suitable form because it intensifies ethnic antagonisms instead of eliminating them. This was very evident even in the case of Yugoslav Federation according to the Constitution from 1974, that in the last decade plus a year or two, which practically functioned more as a confederation. Today everyone can see the results of such functioning." Two points. First, I must suggest to you that to all those states Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which exist happily as confederations, the suggestion that confederations intensify antagonisms is not founded and/or absurd but is your way of justifying Serbia's refusal of confederation offers made by other states at earlier times and in particular at The Hague Conference. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are not right. Confederation is a historically outdated form. All confederations, including United States and Switzerland, have grown to become federations and there was no reverse processes where federations became confederations. There were no such processes in history.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are alternative arguments but I don't have time. But let's look at the next sentence, because this really tells the truth, doesn't it, Professor, if we bear in mind that the first possibility, the optimum choice, is gone, that you're against confederation and you say this: "Second choice is an independent and sovereign state of Serbia which would comprise all Serbian countries which are in geographical continuity, thus connected territorially. To go over that and demand that state also encompass the Serbian majority countries which are separated from the mother country Serbia by territory where the second nation represents majority is only possible by entering war with the risk of confronting the organised international community and exposing to its draconian sanctions." Now, you will have to look at it again. It may need some revision in its translation, but you're telling us you were a mere technical draftsman, assisting without being asked in the drafting of constitutions, and you're here saying that the second choice involving territories where the second nation represents the majority, and that has to be Muslims and Croats, is only possible by entering war. You're simply describing exactly what this accused did when he led people to their fates in an attempt to bring about a Serbian country in geographical continuity. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not correct, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to us.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You keep ignoring the fact that I wrote this in my capacity as a scholar who held no public office at the time. In this article, I explain what two options for solving the Serbian national issue are possible. I chose the optimum one as the federal state option. As for the second option, I said that it was not possible to realise because it would have to come at the cost of confrontation with the international community and exposing the country to Draconian sanctions. Therefore, the second option was not realistic, could not have been realised. This is not a pogrom at all, this is simply my view as a scholar which I expressed ex cathedra.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, I notice on the first page you're identified as the author and as Judge of the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia. Was your judgeship a factor in the writing of this article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. You know, in our journals, various errors occur. This is one of the obvious errors. At the time, I was no longer a Judge of the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia because, quite simply, the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia existed no longer at the time. But in front of my name you can see the term "Professor." I am a professor of the faculty of law in Belgrade, and they simply did not update the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Frankly, I was surprised to see the reference to your being a judge. But could you tell us why that second choice was only possible by what is described here as entering war, by waging war? Why, in your view, was it only possible through the waging of a war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely because the Serbian people, against their will, were taken to live in other independent national states. Serbian people were separated from their parent state. Up until that time, Serbian people lived in one state and then by ways of secession and war, Serbian people were taken to live in another state, and that fact was recognised by the international community. Therefore, through secessionist acts and armed action, Serbian people were taken to live in another state. The international community recognised that, and by doing so it severed the Serbian nation into several bits. The Serbs, up until that time, lived in one state, in federal Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can go to English page 5, to page 377 for you, Professor Markovic, to have some feel for how your approach to the other states may have informed your judgement, note this: You asserted that: "... the advocacy of one state is not enough to preserve a multiethnic state. The Serbs and Serbia could not prevent leaving Yugoslavia by the people and republics that want to found independent and sovereign states." But then this: "It is very likely those nations entered the joint state of Yugoslavia with calculation finding it as a necessary evil on the way to constitution of their own statehood. Thus, first Yugoslavia was their salvation from the German outvoting and assimilation -" no surprise to the Slovenes, Croats, and Muslims - "and thanks to the federal system and criterion on which it was executed the second one was a radical step forward on the way to the realisation of the final goal." So that the second Yugoslavia, this is between the two wars of the last century, "... was incubation for those people of secessionism which broke out when relevant social and political consequences fell into place ..." Is it really your view that going back to the Second World War, there was there was a plan on the part of Slovenes and Croats, executed by their successors, to achieve independence via the bridge of Yugoslavia? Is that really your case -- not your case, your belief?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why you are bringing up the Second World War. I don't see the Second World War mentioned here at all. You are placing my statement into a wrong temporal context. I am here referring to the creation of the common kingdom, the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes. There is no mention of the Second World War here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But is it your belief that there was a planned use of Yugoslavia as a bridge by Slovenian and Croatian politicians eventually to obtain their independence? Is that what you're saying? And also the Muslims in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me about my personal view, then, yes, this is my belief to this day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to page 6, and in your text, that will be picking up at the halfway down page 377. And we can see your views, your emerging views on the other nations and republics -- yes, republics. "Such a federal system based on the quasi ethnic criterion was the best leavening for secessionism. Convenient motive for it to break out was found in the aspiration of Serbia to correct its humiliating constitutional position in the federation established in the period from 1968 to 1974. Constitution from 1974 established Serbia as a republic of the second class." I then miss a couple of sentences without disservice, I hope. "Two Serbian provinces which were the rival-countries to their state Serbia had been supported by the republics which became the secessionist ones later. What is more, they were encouraged in their emancipation and secessionism by Serbia. According to them, it was a condition for ethnic and political balance in the multiethnic Yugoslavia. When the political forces grew up in Serbia so that they were able to establish the republic statehood in the whole republic territory -" and then this - "as well as in other republics on the federal Yugoslavia ..." That phrase is a reference to the RSK and to the RS, isn't it? You're linking the establishment of the RS and the RSK to the developments in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite wrong, Mr. Nice. It's obvious that you misunderstood the matters. There is reference here to other republics that had the status of federal units. No Republic of Serbian Krajina, whatsoever. Anyone who knew the facts at the time could not have made such a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's read on. "... that project was explained to the world as an aspiration for creation of Greater Serbia." Well, forgive my getting it wrong and I'm only too happy to be corrected, whether it's a matter of interpretation or otherwise, how can something being explained to the world as an aspiration for a Greater Serbia be other than the connection of Serbia with other territories and particularly other Serb territories?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The non-aspiration -- it is not the aspiration for uniting the Serb territories but, rather, the aspiration for establishing the single state in Serbia in its entire territory in accordance with the 1974 constitution. There is no aspiration towards other republics' territories, no. The reference here is the reference to the autonomous provinces within the Republic of Serbia, which grew together with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's read on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think I understand this answer, Mr. Nice. I wonder if I can ask a question. Going back to the sentence which begins, "When the political forces grew up in Serbia so that they were able to establish the republic statehood in the whole republic territory -" now, I understand that to be a reference to the autonomous provinces, but it then goes on to say - "as well as in other republics of the federal Yugoslavia." So reading short, they were able to establish the republic statehood in other republics of the federal Yugoslavia. Now, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This must be a translation error. This is a misunderstanding. Just like in other republics of the federal Yugoslavia, the reference here is to the fact that all other federal republics in Yugoslavia have prerogatives, state prerogatives in their entire territory except for the Republic of Serbia, which had state prerogatives only in the territory outside the provinces. So in that sense, the desire here is to give an equal standing to Serbia, the same status that other federal republics had. This must be some miscommunication due to wrong translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it from that answer, Professor, you accept that if it's an accurate translation, then it describes the situation that Mr. Nice was presenting to you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice is advancing an argument that the Republic of Serbia wanted to establish statehood in its ethnic territory. What I claim is that it wanted to establish statehood in its republican territory. This is the essential difference between Mr. Nice's view and my view. He's claiming one thing, and I'm claiming quite the opposite.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we'll see how you deal with this same proposition with some later passages in this article, Professor, but let's stick with where we are. "Serbia in the whole republic territory outside which almost the third of Serbs was left in other republics is really big in regard to the rest South-Slav republics. Precisely in that is the main failure and inadequacy of the political project which is called Yugoslavia for the Serbian people. Regardless of how much the Serbian people are divided into more federal units, Serbia will always be big in such Yugoslavia and will give complexes to others. First of all to those who do not have its history and historical glory, the Croats and Slovenes who are like that in front of the others and then to those who generated their quasi ethnic autochthonism from the Serbian national feeling what is the case with Macedonians and Muslims." This shows your set of mind, Professor Markovic. The Slovenes and the Croats lacked Serbs' history and historical glory, and the quasi-ethnic autochthonism of Macedonians and Muslims was not worthy of taking into account. You show in this passage, I suggest to you, an absolute belief in the superiority of Serbs. Am I not right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not right at all. This is a well-known case, case well known in the world of federalism, namely that one federal unit which stands out in view of its size, number of residents, history, is a thorn in the side of other federal units. That was the case with Prussia in the German federation starting in 1871. That was the case with Russia within the Soviet federation from 1922 or, rather, 1924 onwards. Therefore, one federal unit which, in terms of its size, historical past and so on is such that it differs from other federal units causes distrust or inspires distrust, and in that sense we can view the thesis of Mr. Lazar Kolisevski that the Yugoslav federation was structured in such a way as to implement the principle "weak Serbia, strong Yugoslavia." Therefore, only if Serbia is deprived of its advantages, and that was the purpose of autonomous provinces, would it become equal with other republics. It would no longer stand out. It would no longer be larger than the rest of the federal republics. This is the essence of my claim. It has no racist or chauvinist views as you are attributing to me. Simply speaking, Serbia was much larger than other units, and unlike other units, it had a very diverse and rich historical past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a lot of understanding for this type of debate and exchange of views between one university professor and his counterpart, but I would like to draw your attention to the time. If Mr. Nice is allowed to continue -- to continue until the end of this session, he would have had six and a half sessions altogether, and please bear in mind that I also need some time for redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am quite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very much so, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I am aware of that, but this is extremely important evidence, and I was aware that the Bench itself was interested in exploring the significance of the constitutional matters, and I'm going to try and complete this article and to take you to an article of criticism of the professor and then deal with Rambouillet, if I may. I realise it's trespassing over the normal period of time, but in my respectful submission it's probably justified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you have taken a very long time in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I have, because the witness has -- the witness has been giving answers of a very particular type, but, Your Honour, can we see how we go with this article, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'd like to get an estimate as to when you plan to finish because the accused rightly says that he wants to re-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I shall finish this article in 10 or 15 minutes. There is an article of criticism which I'd invite you again to consider reading over the interval, which you may not be prepared to do so, and then I'll simply use whatever time is available before re-examination time starts for the witness to get away today, if that's acceptable to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, how much time would you need for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At least one hour. And even then, I will not have had too much time as compared to Mr. Nice. It would not have been an unproportional division of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Bear in mind that in re-examination you can only ask questions on issues that arise out of the cross-examination. It's not an opportunity to examine the witness again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I have in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll consult. We'll probably have to put a limit on the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you have up until the first 15 minutes of the next session, so the accused will have three-quarters of an hour for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will have to deal with things more swiftly on this article. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honours please. I will have to invite you to look at this article in more depth perhaps privately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 7, for the witness page 378. End of the first paragraph. Professor Markovic, what you're saying, incidentally, I suggest to you, is intentionally incorrect on many occasions. Look what you say here. You say: "... the separation cannot realise the territories in which the majority population which did not commit itself to leaving Yugoslavia lives. In that case, the republic borders which are conditional anyway will no longer be valid and they are valid only if there is a federal system and territorial integrity of Yugoslavia. In that case, exclusively the ethnic borders are relevant." That's the clearest possible intention to redraw the borders. Am I not right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. This is a unanimous view of the scholars. The borders were drawn between federal units provisionally, and they reflected the organisation of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia. They were created up to the second session of AVNOJ in 1943. Marshal of Yugoslavia, Josip Broz, used to say that the borders between republics resemble fine lines in marble. They do not separate but to the -- to the contrary, they unite. Therefore, these borders were drawn only within the federal system in order to exercise the right of the peoples to self-determination. And this is a unanimous view of all scholars within Yugoslavia. There is not a single legal document establishing the borders between units. And why is it so? Because these are the borders reflecting the organisation of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia. Its central committee, regional committees, and provincial committees. So this is just a reflection of those borders, whereas the legal borders were never established pursuant to a referendum or pursuant to a legal document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll cut right to several points I would like to draw to the Chamber's attention. We'll come to page 12 in the English, and for you, Professor, it will be page 383. The large paragraph for you, Professor, and towards the bottom of the page on the English, and you said this: "To put it very briefly, in the present circumstances the joint state of ... Montenegro is, like an extension of the SFRY, the preservation of the parent core of the Serbian people and their statehood. It is not the state of all Serbs. In that sense, in terms of that request, its better achievement is a federal Yugoslavia of all constituent Yugoslav nations. However, we saw why that idea is unattainable. Better to say, its realisation is unacceptable for the Serbs. Likewise, there is no need to insist on a sovereign state of Serbia, when Montenegro wishes to build a federal state with Serbia." Then this: "That federal state is a core around which the Serbian countries would gather and it would serve as a base for by-stages unification of the Serbian countries and the Serbian people. We are primarily talking about the areas where the Serbian people is in majority in Croatia and Bosnia, and partly in Macedonia too." There's more of it on the following pages, but, Professor, what you're setting out there is exactly what was this accused's intention, that by stages Serb areas of Croatia and Bosnia should link with the motherland. It couldn't be clearer.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for this compliment on clarity. However, it has nothing whatsoever to do with any kind of joint action with Mr. Milosevic. I have to reiterate again here. I am presenting my academic opinion, my scientific opinion, no political position at all. This is an academic article published in a scientific journal. We can have an academic debate on it, but not a legal one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just tell us what you meant --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us what you meant --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- is something that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us what you meant if you didn't mean that you're setting out what's to happen in the future, that Serb territories of Croatia and Bosnia are to link up with Serbia. Tell us what you did mean.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a ideal request, aspiration that Germany, Italy before the unification had at some point. It's not a political demand. It's a programme, it's an idea, it's a vision of a man who is dealing with these matters, how the Serbian issue, national issue, can be resolved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you assisted unasked to -- in the drafting of the 1992 Serbian constitution, who gave you ideas as to what sort of really important constitutional elements should go in this constitution? Who gave you the ideas or did they all come from your own brain?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying again I'm not the author of the entire constitution, and I apologise to the people who contributed to the making of that constitution in advance. You make me seem like I am claiming to be the single and only author. There was a platform for the reform of the political system, and we referred to that document in order to identify ideas that influenced the making of the 1990 constitution. That platform for the reform of the political system is in evidence here, and it exposed, enumerated various ideas on what the political order and system should be in the future. The constitution of 1990 implemented them. The commission appointed by the Presidency identified these views.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at one part of the 1992 constitution, and one part only, Article 2. Page 4. And the document was also exhibited as Exhibit 319, tab 2. We just need to look very briefly at Article 2. Article 2, please. Thank you very much. We see Article 2 says this, the second part: "The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia may be joined by other member republics, in accordance with the present constitution." Which member republics were you referring to? Was that to Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina? Was it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. We're talking about a type of open federation. There are two types of federation in the world; closed federations with the structure determined in advance, then unchangeable, and open federations that are opened to new members subject to the decision of the Federal Assembly. That is written in Article 78 of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The RS and the RSK were declared or declared themselves as republics, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see absolutely no connection with Article 2 of the constitution of Yugoslavia. How can you know their intention in advance?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go now, then, please, to the article that I've asked you to review several days ago, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, may the article the witness has just gone through be exhibited, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will admit the last document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 824.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we've already seen, I think, in the constitution of the RS and the RSK their powers to unite elsewhere. If we now look at an article written by Slobodan Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if the Chamber still has the copies that were distributed or if they've handed them back. Let's just look at -- does the witness have this? It's in English. Comes from the European Studies Centre. He's read it, I hope.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first thing we can notice about this article, Professor, is it's written by Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the first thing you can notice. And second, I can tell you it was written by non-lawyers. Mr. Samardzic never graduated from the law school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Samardzic is a much respected intellectual, is he not, or won't you have that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not deny that. I am just denying the assumption that somebody without graduating from the law school can debate a legal issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we go to page 2 of 11, halfway down the page we can see that this is by no means written by people who are friends of the ICTY or any Western conspiracy, because the author describes NATO's intervention as the recent "brutal, illegal, and illegitimate military intervention of the NATO forces against the country." So you would accept that this is a Serb without any particular leaning towards the forces and powers that established this Tribunal. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only agree that this man is humane enough to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we go to endnotes 18 and 19, we see that -- we see the material upon which they -- author relies. We see references in 18 and 19 to Slobodan Vucetic, who was, what, in the Constitutional Court? Correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not a member of the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia that I was a member of. He is currently a member of the Constitutional Court of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the man Cavoski, or Cavoski probably. Cavoski, I think -- no, I was right the first time, Cavoski, just again so that we can have a flavour of the sources relied on, Cavoski is the founder member of one of the Save Radovan Karadzic organisations, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kosta Cavoski is one of the first fighters for political pluralism in the Republic of Serbia, and he was among the founders and the inner circle of leadership of the Democratic Party. This is what I would say of him rather than what you said: He is one of the forefront fighters for political democracy in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see that you're referred to in footnote number 9. Elsewhere but certainly in footnote number 9. If we get a shape of the document, but if we come back to the top of the page, Usher, please, page 5 of 11 -- in fact the bottom of that page, this is the assertion made by this group in respect of the constitutions and the operation of the constitutions that you helped in constructing. Five lines up from the bottom of the page: "What does make Serbia different from the other post-communist countries of Central and Eastern Europe is that the President relies heavily on one political party and on this basis the principle of party leadership is directly transformed into the principle of state leadership. This establishes a firm ruling amalgam between the Parliament, the Government, and the head of state, who in reality most often act outside the constitution. This amalgam of power existed before the constitution was adopted in the form of an all-powerful party, and its leader, that adopted constitution tailored to its own needs and simply moved itself into the new institutions. It continues to function even now, when the strong party chief is no longer President of Serbia, but President of Yugoslavia." Well, the time of which the author's writing includes the time when you were both Assembly member and Deputy Prime Minister. Is his analysis of the reality of the operation of your constitutions or the constitutions in which you gave some assistance accurate? Professor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you hear the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm without translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I heard the remark of the interpreter in Serbian saying that the interpreter did not understand the end of Mr. Nice's question. Since they didn't understand the end of Mr. Nice's question, they were unable to interpret it. I heard the interpreter saying that he or she did not understand the end of Mr. Nice's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time that this article was written or over the time -- I'll go back. The time to which this article refers was the time when you were an Assembly member and later a Deputy Prime Minister, and I'm asking you is his analysis of the reality of the operation of your constitutions correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't have the text in my own language. I have it in English. But all right, I'm not going to make an issue out of this. So I'm looking at the English version. As far as I'm able to understand and as far as I understand your question, he objects here to the fact that the head of state is at the same time the party chief. But the same thing happens today. Borisav Tadic is the leader of the Democratic Party, and at the same time the head of state. If that is not what you meant by your question, you have to edify me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few more questions on this article because of time. Page 7 of 11, if you please, in the middle of the page. A particular challenge to the interaction of your two principal drafting exercises in the 1990 constitution of Serbia and the 1992. Second sentence: "By failing to bring its constitution in line -- into line with the Federal Constitution, Serbia has retained powers, which constitutionally belong to the federation. This has forced Montenegro to do the same and the federal organs therefore exercises its constitutional powers to only a limited extent. From 1992 to 1997 the president of Serbia in fact conducted Yugoslavia's foreign policy, which should be conducted by the federal government. The same person continues to conduct foreign policy following his election as president of the federal state, although this is equally unconstitutional." Do you accept he's right about this being unconstitutional for the President of Serbia to conduct the federal foreign policy?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of 1992, the -- the internal and foreign policies are charted and implemented by the government. This statement here is not substantiated by any document, and it is completely wrong to say that despite the existence of the federal government politicians from other countries came to speak to Mr. Milosevic, not the federal Prime Minister. But they knew their reasons for doing that, for not going to see the federal Prime Minister rather than Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the accused run the foreign policy for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or not? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The federal government. The federal government ran the foreign policy, although it is the president of the Republic of Serbia who had the most contacts with the representatives of the international community, but they insisted on speaking to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we are four or five minutes beyond the break, and in view of the fact that we have to stop at a quarter to, those four or five minutes will have to be taken from the 15 minutes allocated to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Otherwise we would eat into the time allocated to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question about the article we were looking at is that it asserts the constitution was a smokescreen for unlimited power, and in a footnote says that in 1987, the federal parliament sat for less than ten effective days. Is he right that you only sat for ten effective days? You'll find it in endnote 4, but you can remember. Did you only sit for ten effective days? We're very pressed for time. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, because I was not an MP in the federal parliament at the time. I told you I was an MP there until 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And as Deputy Prime Minister, you have no idea how often the Assembly met, do you? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not asking me about the republican Assembly. You're asking me about the federal Assembly. I was Deputy Prime Minister in the republican government, not the federal government. I didn't count the days when the federal Assembly was in session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help us with this: We're going to hear in due course, as already in evidence, of the millions of dollars or financial equivalent that went to support the RS and the RSK military forces. In either of your capacities, were you ever informed about that or was it kept from you? Were you informed? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about it, and I don't know who would have the obligation to provide me with such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, as a citizen, are you not entitled to know where your taxes are going, broadly?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we have such rights as citizens. However, there is a distribution of work in the government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a parliamentarian are you entitled to know where the money goes?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that is expressed on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a Deputy Prime Minister, are you entitled to know where the money goes?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was Deputy Prime Minister in the republican government, whereas the army is financed from the federal budget.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're really telling us, so that we can have this on our record, you were never told by anyone of the 30th and 40th personnel centres until I mentioned it to you today?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that under oath, that I heard this for the first time this morning from you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the criticisms we've seen in the article, you've also been heavily and publicly criticised by a lawyer from your own university, different department, Stefan Lilic. He's in an article on the constitution headed The Unbearable Lightness of Unconstitutional Being, he's also heavily criticised you publicly for the quality of your latest constitutional book which your students were obliged to work from and which took no account of any of the recent developments in the former Yugoslavia. It's correct, isn't it, that you've been subject to heavy public criticism from that person?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He criticised me because I did not update the textbook with changes in the constitution, and I was waiting for the amendments in the constitution of Serbia. I updated the latest edition. The new constitution of Serbia was pending, and I waited for that to update the textbook. However, since the amendments had not been passed until then, I published the ninth latest edition of the textbook, taking into account all the changes in the legislation of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... criticisms and their replies by this witness to them are available if they would help the Chamber in assessing them. Tab 47 of the witness's exhibits is described as the Contact Group Non-negotiable Principles of 22nd of January of 1999, and it ends with, "Kosovo consent required inter alia for changes to borders and declaration of martial law." For some reason the last part wasn't included. It's now on display and we see that in fact the non-negotiable principles, as described, included "Judicial protection for human rights," and then "Role of OSCE," and under, "Implementation" "Dispute resolution mechanism, establishment of a joint commission, participation of OSCE and other international bodies as necessary." First of all, can you explain why the exhibit you produced was incomplete?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there was talk only about principles not the entire document. We were talking only about the principles, the general elements, and you are talking about the document as a whole, which was not contested. We believe that the principles endorsed by the Contact Group under the title "General Elements," we thought that on the basis of these principles an agreement should be made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- no. The question is why the Judges were presented with a document that was incomplete. In stopping at "Kosovo consent required inter alia for changes to borders and declaration of martial law," in the copy provided to them and to me, did you intentionally cut off the last bit about human rights and implementation? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite intentionally because that was not the subject of the discussion. The subject was the principles for the Contact Group, what you see here, general elements, not the entire document. That is what was being negotiated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The full document, which should have been available to this Court, makes it quite clear from the beginning, as you all understood, that there was going to be an international presence and that meant an international military presence and so all this arguing about the military element being the cause of the problem is false. You always knew there was going to be an international military presence before this accused signed up to engage in the agreement at all, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are absolutely wrong. I was the entire time in the castle in Rambouillet, and I know for a fact as well as all the other participants of that gathering there was not a word of mention of military presence. Only on the last day of the negotiations was it notified to the parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please remind yourself of this document, which is -- our Exhibit 135, I think. If it can go on the overhead projector. This is the letter you wrote on the 23rd of February. Let's read it. It went to Ambassadors Hill, Petritsch and Mayorski. "The delegation of the government of Republic of Serbia wishes to emphasise ..." Next paragraph: "We would particularly like to emphasise the same as the Contract Group, no independence of Kosovo and Metohija." Next paragraph: "All elements of self-government at the time of defining of the agreement have to be known and clearly defined." Next paragraph: "The FRY agree to discuss the scope and character of international presence in Kosmet to implement the agreement to be accepted in Rambouillet. The FR of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Serbia are fully ready to continue the work in line with the positive spirit of this meeting. We therefore consider that it would be useful to set a reasonable deadline..." et cetera. Until you were supplanted in the negotiations by Milutinovic, you, A, knew that there was going to be an international military presence, and B, until you were supplanted you were happy to go on negotiating, weren't you? And this letter makes it absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it makes clear absolutely the opposite. What is being referred to is the presence of the international forces, not NATO forces. And only in Kosovo, not the entire territory of Serbia. Linguistically speaking, what you are reading does not show what you want to show. It speaks of the presence of international forces, not international military forces, not international troops. International forces concerned a civilian mission and only to Kosmet, not the entire territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice -- Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I also receive a copy of this document that is being discussed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And when did you write this letter? Was it after you were given the deadline, noon of 23rd of February?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was precisely the time of it, towards the end of the conference, three hours after -- 3.00 in the afternoon on the 23rd of February, in Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what you were asking at that time was an extension of that deadline. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The deadline was extended without a request from us. It was extended twice before that, on the 14th of February and the 20th of February. But it was said that the negotiations on the agreement were to be continued in Paris at a time that we would be informed of subsequently, because we expressed the readiness to continue the talks in Paris and to attend those talks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, your last answer before the question by His Honour is simply unrealistic and takes no account of reality. There'd already been the OSCE mission. There had been the KDOM mission. These didn't work. It was known -- and there had been an escalation of violence. It was known that there was going to be a military component and this agreement or this plan for agreement was exactly based on the Dayton model. You all knew there was going to be a military presence and you were going along with it until this accused stopped you. And he stopped you between Rambouillet and Paris, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're just not right on that score and that that is so I'm going to show you the conclusions enacted by the national assembly when it sent its delegation to Rambouillet to negotiate. May I be allowed to show these conclusions on the overhead projector? Just one sentence, in fact of that document. That sentence, it is the conclusion of the national assembly, and the mandate finds the Rambouillet delegation and it states: "We do not accept the presence or agree to the presence of foreign troops on our territory under any pretext what -- of the implementation of the agreement reached." That is the sentence. It is one of the conclusions dated the 4th of February before we actually went to Rambouillet. So what Mr. Nice just said, to put it mildly, just -- is just not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your description of the whole process of the 1998 negotiations and of the Rambouillet process is completely incorrect. There was goodwill on the side of the internationals and before that there was a willingness to consult on the part of the Kosovo Albanians. Did you record the evidence of Zoran Lilic when he was before this Tribunal on this topic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I cannot follow all the proceedings at this Tribunal because I have to teach at the university.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you follow the evidence of Ambassador Petritsch?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, although I do know Ambassador Petritsch. I didn't hear what he said in testimony before this Tribunal. As I say, these proceedings take place in the morning when I have business to attend to at the university.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far as the accused is concerned, we've heard evidence from Borisav Jovic of his complete domination of and power over the party. Do you agree with that characterisation of him in general terms? You were a member of the party throughout and a founder member.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: Every party leader dominates his party. So he is a leader. He is the first man of the party, the leader of the party. I don't know of any party where the party president is not a leader.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... you went back to Belgrade on the 23rd of February and that's when -- to see the accused, no doubt, and that's when things all changed. Is he right about that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is right inasmuch as one fact and that is that on the 23rd we returned to Belgrade because it was when the conference in Rambouillet ended. As to the second point, no, he's not right there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just two other questions. Is it right that when in 1996 local elections were apparently lost as a result of fraud by the SPS, the accused turned to you for assistance, and eventually of course, you all accepted the reality of electoral fraud in what's called the lex specialis that was drafted that gave the vote or gave the decision to the opposition parties? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That law was adopted by the national Assembly at the time, and there are only two articles and it was positively assessed by the group led by Mr. Gonzales and generally by the international community as a whole. They gave a very good assessment of the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, because I see the time, going right back to the beginning of your evidence, 1989, the amendments, so far as those amendments concerned Vojvodina - of course Kosovo had fallen into an entirely different organisation and regime - as far as those amendments for Vojvodina, were they reversed by an omnibus law for Vojvodina in the last few years?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That law merely defined more precisely the provisions of Article 109 of the constitution and it was called the omnibus law in popular terms. It specified the regions in which the autonomous province, according to Article 109 of the constitution, has normative powers, and then it stated which those questions were that the autonomous province can regulate on the basis of its own laws or, rather, I apologise, by its normative acts. It did not step outside the frameworks of the constitutional provisions and solutions. It merely defined more precisely the provisions of Article 109 of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The question of exhibits can be dealt with either today or tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson. I shall try to be brief and use my time as rationally as possible, although I highly doubt that I'll be able to get through everything I want to get through, but unfortunately it is the physical restrictions of time here. Re-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Markovic, at the beginning of the cross-examination, Mr. Nice asked you whether you had taken part in the working group which, according to my instructions and Tudjman's instructions, was supposed to divide up Bosnia. And then he provided us with an exhibit, an extract from a book, in fact, by Professor Avramov, in which she states the following, and my question to you is this, or, rather, does that reflect what actually happened, what was going on at the time? She says this, and it is on page 140. There's a number, 140, in the documents I received from Mr. Nice. I don't have the pagination, but 111 is the final -- the final digits of the ERN number. It says: "The presidents of the two republics, Tudjman and Milosevic, undertook another step but this time not an official step. They established two teams with the aim of comprehensively reviewing the political, economic, constitutional, legal, and international legal consequences of a possible disintegration of Yugoslavia and through that prism to seek a solution to it. Most probably the decision about this was taken at the meeting between the two leaders in Karadjordjevo in March 1991." And then she goes on to state the following: "Unfortunately, this attempt was not successful. The only point on which the two parties agreed was that the main determinant for the talks must be 70 years of life in common, life together, and stands on all other issues were very far divergent." Therefore, Professor Markovic, when you talked to your colleagues, did anybody ever mention any division of Bosnia-Herzegovina at all?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I state on oath, having taken the solemn declaration at the beginning of this testimony, that there was not one single word about Bosnia-Herzegovina's division. Not one single word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, let me be even more specific. We're not now dealing with your talks with your Croatian colleagues but your own internal group consultations and agreements, the team mentioned here in fact, the team that is said to have taken part on the Serb side. Did you amongst yourselves ever mention any idea about Bosnia's division in any way? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How would we have the authority and power to do so?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about your power mandate. I'm asking you whether you ever brought an idea like that up. Did you discuss it amongst yourselves ever?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either not amongst ourselves. We never discussed this. What we did discuss was what Professor Avramov stresses in her book. That's what we discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what Smilja Avramov says here, "comprehensive review of the political, economic, constitutional, legal and international legal aspects," is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was the subject of your talks, was it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With my partner, and that was Professor Smiljko Sokol, who is professor of constitutional law at the faculty of law in Zagreb, I discussed with him constitutional and legal problems, and international legal problems, as Professor Avramov says, economics ones. Academician Kosta Mihailovic, we all discussed that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you're testifying about coincides fully with what Professor Avramov writes in her book. Now, look at the next page, please, the central paragraph towards the end. It is four lines from the bottom. It says: "The fact remains --" The explanation is given, et cetera, of how the talks were conducted. "The fact remains," she says, "that the discussion was waged behind closed doors, far from the eyes of the public, but there were never any secret agreements nor was there anything which should be hidden from public view. It was just one episode in the attempt to find a solution which would not even be worth mentioning had stories not been brought up in the press which have nothing to do with reality." Is that the proper assessment, the one made by Professor Avramov? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That corresponds to the truth in all its aspects based on the quotations you have just given us, and that working group had, I think, only two successful meetings and one meeting planned but never -- one that never took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now we have to go as fast as possible, Professor. Do you happen to know that for an entire year, one year after that famous meeting in Karadjordjevo and independent of that meeting, of course, but I'm talking chronologically here, that for a whole year after that meeting, alleged agreement on Bosnia's division, the Serb side in Bosnia-Herzegovina accepted Cutileiro's plan which enabled a peaceful settlement to the problem and an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the fact that it was one year after Karadjordjevo that the Serb side came out in favour of Cutileiro's plans, doesn't that deny and negate the idea of me and Tudjman having an agreement on Bosnia's division?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those two facts are completely at odds with each other. Cutileiro's plan for Bosnia implies the whole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Markovic, we all know about the Cutileiro plan, but tell me this now, please: Since you were not able to remember the Belgrade initiative awhile ago, Professor Rakic, during the break -- as this was brought up by Mr. Nice in the first place, Professor Rakic has given me some documents here, the text, in fact, as far as I remember, in Belgrade the 16th of September, 1991 is the date and venue, and I'm going to hand it over to you. And would the usher be so kind as to place this --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If he wasn't present at the negotiations, if he has no memory of it, what has the document got to do with it? It's not his document. When the witness asserted lack of recollection of these things, this one in particular, I moved on. I'm not sure that this is appropriate re-examination of any kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He may be able to, but let me hear the question that you're putting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I had in mind the fact that Professor Markovic, when this was mentioned, said, yes, I know about it but I haven't got the documents for me to be able to answer, so I'm providing him with the document and I wish to go through the document very briefly. Mr. Nice explained, et cetera --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you all got this text of the Belgrade initiative, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I've been provided with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, from this text can we see that the representatives of the republics -- of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we take it in alphabetical order, Montenegro and Serbia, that they had jointly asserted basic grounds for relationships in Yugoslavia? Can we see that and that is the title of the document, in fact?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it emanates from the preamble itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, from this document is it quite clear that the representatives of the three republics are speaking about the basis for structuring relations in Yugoslavia as it is made up six republics but that the initiatives were made by the three republics in question? Is that quite obvious?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would emerge from point 1 of I.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Professor Markovic. This initiative provides the groundwork for relations in Yugoslavia to be regulated. I point 1 it says Yugoslavia is the joint state of equal republics, nations, and citizens. Was that the approach that was the principled approach, the constitutional, legal position taken by the Republic of Serbia herself? That is to say Yugoslavia joint state of equal republics and citizens, nations and citizens?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was Serbia's approach, that Yugoslavia as a federal state in which all the Serbs were rallied together and gathered together should be preserved as a state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Markovic, in point 5 -- I don't have time to go through the entire document, but let's take point 5 of the first chapter. It says the republics and nations of Yugoslavia can step down from Yugoslavia in the way and methodology established by the constitution and laws of Yugoslavia but they cannot violate the interests of other nations and republics by doing so. Is that the position taken generally in the political life of the country with respect to the principled approach that Serbia adopted?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the position of the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia as well as we have seen. So they were able to step down or secede from Yugoslavia but only according to the methodology prescribed by the constitution without violating the rights and interests of the other nations and republics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And take a look at point 7 now, further down, which begins as follows: "Yugoslavia is founded upon the equality of the Yugoslav nations and republics." And then it goes on to say: "The national minorities are recognised all national and human rights established by corresponding international covenants." Was that the principled stand that Serbia had which it advocated both in the amendments of the constitution and in enacting the 1992 constitution itself later on when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was established as being a continuity with the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was Serbia's approach, and these two points or, rather, the two sentences that you read out were taken over directly from the decisions of the second session of the AVNOJ, the AVNOJ. Both those things exist in the decisions made by the second session of AVNOJ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now take a look at point 9. It says: "A market economy, equality in property, the freedom of people and property, capital and knowledge, entrepreneurial undertaking shall be the groundworks for the economic life of Yugoslavia ..." et cetera, et cetera. Was that the stand of principle taken by the leadership of Serbia as well and the Republic of Serbia in attempting to solve the Yugoslav crisis in its approach to the crisis?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republic of Serbia did have this position not only to preserve Yugoslavia but to transform the constitutional system of Yugoslavia in keeping with a market economy and its principles and the principle of political pluralism and parliamentrism, the parliamentary system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you've said that, please bear in mind point 10 of these basic principles: "In Yugoslavia, state authorities organised on the division of power in the form of multi-party parliamentary republics based on the rule of law and social justice." Was that the approach that Serbia took, the position Serbia took?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the ideas and ideals that the Republic of Serbia based the transformation of the Yugoslav state on, and they gained expression in the 1992 constitution because all this is the principle set out in the basic provisions of the 1992 constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now please take a look is what is stated about the relations within Yugoslavia in the second chapter of this document. Item 1: "Republics and nations of Yugoslavia base their relations on common interests and respect and protection of their interests on mutual respect and cooperation." Is that in principle the position taken by Yugoslavia -- by Serbia in the Yugoslav crisis?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All aimed at preserving Yugoslavia as a federal state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These are effectively all leading questions. What's being done is the witness is being reminded of a text without my having cross-examined on the text, and if I had been allowed the opportunity to cross-examine on this text, believe me I would have had things to say. And about its -- the way it fits with other events. But if we look at the questions, all that's being done is it's being used as a vehicle for a leading question of a kind that the witness picks up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I don't know that this is taking us very far. You should move on to something else. I think you have been through this document sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us just clarify another matter, since we said that there was division of power, competencies among Yugoslav organs. Item 3 speaks about the Assembly of Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we have dealt with this document sufficiently. Let's move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a peculiarity that I would like to quote to Professor Markovic from this document. I would like to remind him of this. On page 5, on page 5 of this document, when speaking of the president of the republic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Bring that to his attention and then move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would just like to draw his attention to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is stated in this initiative, in this document, that the president of the republic is elected by the Assembly of Yugoslavia for each term of office from another republic at the proposal of that republic in an A, B, C chronology of the names of the republics. So each time a president is elected from another republic following the A, B, C order. So the first president to be elected in this manner would be a president from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Are you familiar with the idea and with the fact that at the time it was proposed that Alija Izetbegovic should be the president of that Yugoslavia as envisaged by this initiative?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This emanates from this provision. That same principle was applied to the chairmanship of the Presidency of SFRY in the 1974 constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, a general question which I would like to link to Mr. Nice's statement, claim on the division of Bosnia from Karadjordjevo. This Belgrade initiative which came six months after the alleged division of Bosnia, because that was in March and this is in September, does it deny any thought of division of Bosnia because it supports the continuity of Yugoslavia? So is that clear, Professor Markovic, based on your knowledge of constitutional legal principles and the contents of this initiative as I've put it to you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one doesn't need to be a constitutional law expert to answer this. One just needs to link certain matters. This document speaks of a united, single Bosnia-Herzegovina which together with the republics of Serbia and Montenegro creates a federal state. Had Bosnia been divided, it would not have figured here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Markovic. Now I will turn very briefly to a document Mr. Nice dwelt on for quite awhile. This is the last document -- maybe not the last document he gave to us, but at any rate, this is a document that he quoted quite extensively. I don't have that much time. This is the journal entitled Pravni Zivot, Legal Life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll exhibit this document, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean this Belgrade initiative document? Well, certainly, certainly, because Mr. Nice referred to it. Therefore, Legal Life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm reminded that it's not translated, so in accordance with the practice, we'll mark it for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D272 ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Markovic, based on this article of yours published in the Legal Life journal, Mr. Nice quoted quite a lot of sentences from that article. I will now quote the bits that he did not quote, because I have an impression that he quoted that only in order to save himself the trouble of putting quite a lot of questions. Now, please take a look at page 366. And for you gentlemen, it should be in chapter 3 in English of this article. Where you go on to state the following, Professor Markovic. After analysing various elections, options, and so on, in the very beginning of chapter 3 you state: "Yugoslavia, as a common state of South-Slav peoples, is the most logical, the most reasonable, and the best solution for a national question of all South-Slav peoples, especially those who are most intermixed such as is the case with Serbs, Muslims, and Croats." Then I continue without skipping anything. The following sentence is: "It is well said that Yugoslavia is the largest Serbia but also Croatia. Bearing that in mind, the Serbian people committed themselves to Yugoslavia as their state twice in this century." And then the final sentence in this paragraph goes on to say: "Because of that, the Serbian people preferred Yugoslavia to the Independent State Of Serbia, regardless of the impression based on the names of the states that only the independent Serbia was a realisation of the ethnic statehood of the Serbs." So you explain why is it that the Serbs preferred Yugoslavia to Serbia. And then you go on to say: "The fact that Yugoslavia is not a national state of the Serbian people is being neutralised for every South-Slav nation including the Serbian people in the way that according to the ethnic criteria in Yugoslavia is organised as a federal state in which the principle of equality of the peoples and their federal units is implemented. In the higher stage of overcoming the ethnic sensibility, the ethnic identity can be preserved along with the constituting of Yugoslavia as the state of equal citizens and constitutional proclamation and guarantees of the voluminous catalogue of the collective ethnic Croats as well as individuals ones as the members of the nation." And then in the next paragraph you say: "In abstract view that is the kind of state that Yugoslavia is. That is the reason why the official policy in the Republic of Serbia defends preservation of Yugoslavia with such persistence and tries in spite of all secessions that took place in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Yugoslavia to preserve it in the uninterrupted existence." And then you go on to say: "The insistence of Serbia on the uninterrupted existence of Yugoslavia as the state regardless of secession of several federal units made possible that nowadays international and the states subject status of Yugoslavia continued and Yugoslavia continued its existence as a state without any interruption."
